title: The Same Old Complaints: The Political War on Higher Education Never Ends
author: David Schultz
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/Screenshot-2026-07-29-at-12.08.58-PM-680x516.png)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/07/30/the-
same-old-complaints-the-political-war-on-higher-education-never-ends/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/Screenshot-2026-07-29-at-12.08.58-PM-680x516.png)

Photo by [Mick De
Paola](https://unsplash.com/@mickdepaola?utm_source=unsplash&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=creditCopyText)

As colleges prepare for the fall, yet again they are under political attack.
Some say that its standards are eroding. Or a college degree does not prepare
one for a career or a job. The Trump administration red-baits universities,
professors, and students. Others, such as the Washington Post’s [Megan
McArdle, rant](https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/2026/07/19/higher-
education-is-losing-publics-trust/) about the alleged cluelessness of higher
education.

None of these complaints are new. They are part of a long history of diatribes
against higher education by those uncomfortable with change, or who have a
political axe to grind.

Consider some recent events.

The grading fight is real enough right now. [Harvard's faculty
voted](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-05-12/harvard-grade-
inflation-plan-to-limit-a-marks-in-undergrad-classes) in May to cap A grades
at 20 percent of any class starting in 2027, after roughly 60 percent of
undergraduate grades came back A's the year before. The relevance fight is
just as loud: a growing share of employers [are hiring without
degrees](https://majormatch.us/blog/employers-hiring-without-degrees-2026/)
and screening for demonstrated skills instead, on the theory that a diploma
has stopped telling them anything useful. Both feel like symptoms of a
uniquely broken moment. Neither is.

Start with the practicality complaint, because it goes back the furthest. In
1509, the Dutch humanist
[Erasmus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_Praise_of_Folly) published [In
Praise of
Folly](https://myluthernet.luthersem.edu/ICS/icsfs/DesideriusErasmus.pdf?target=adde7995-df62-494a-80c6-5a73aaf3f4f1),
mocking the scholastic theologians who dominated Europe's first universities
for burying “simple truths beneath oceans of technical jargon and
philosophical hairsplitting.” That is a five-hundred-year-old complaint about
tenured scholars and abstract theory, voiced while European universities still
taught in Latin to men training for the priesthood.

The complaint resurfaced with new force in the industrial era. The [Morrill
Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morrill_Land-Grant_Acts) of 1862, which
created the land grant university system, answered a widespread sense that
classical education had become useless for a nation of farmers and mechanics,
directing the new colleges to teach agriculture and the mechanic arts
alongside classical studies. A decade later, the Reverend John A. Anderson,
taking over what became Kansas State, stripped the classical curriculum out
entirely and pledged to fit students for the ordinary pursuits of life.

The other side pushed back just as hard. In 1869, the poet and critic [Matthew
Arnold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_and_Anarchy) published  _Culture
and Anarchy_ , arguing that education's purpose was “pursuit of our total
perfection by means of getting to know, on all the matters which most concern
us, the best which has been thought and said in the world. Writing directly
against the vocational drift of his own era. American education had its own
version of this fight brewing at the same time. [Horace
Mann](https://www.acton.org/religion-liberty/volume-33-number-3/horace-mann-
and-irony-secular-education) built the common school system on the premise
that education existed to produce citizens capable of democratic self-
government, a civic purpose neither purely vocational nor purely classical.

A half century later, [John
Dewey](https://www.johndeweyphilosophy.com/books/democracy_and_education/Vocational_Aspects_of_Education.html)
attacked the vocational-versus-liberal split directly, arguing that treating
practical training and cultural education as opposites was itself the mistake,
since it stigmatized manual work as mindless and academic work as useless.

Every argument since about whether college should train workers or educate
citizens is a rerun of that same unresolved fight, dressed in new clothes:
business majors versus philosophy majors in the 1980s, coding bootcamps versus
the humanities today.

Now to grade inflation, which is older as a named anxiety than most people
assume. In 1894, a Harvard faculty committee calling itself the Committee on
Raising the Standard lamented that “Grades A and B are sometimes given too
readily, Grade A for work of no very high merit, and Grade B for work not far
above mediocrity.” That is Harvard, decades before radio, worrying that its
own faculty had gone soft.

The term itself did not appear until 1972, when sociologist [David
Riesman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Riesman) coined it in a front-
page New York Times story, tracing rising grades to Vietnam-era faculty
reluctant to fail students into the draft. Even that framing treated grade
inflation as new, when Harvard's own faculty had said almost the identical
thing seventy-eight years earlier. By 2001, Harvard's own [Harvey
Mansfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Mansfield) was still fighting
the same battle, calling the grades faculty gave a scandal. Notice the word
still. Each generation of critics writes as though it caught its institution
in a uniquely modern act of dishonesty. Each is, in fact, restating an 1894
memo, which is exactly what Harvard's faculty did again this May.

A third complaint has always run alongside the first two: the fear that the
university is quietly manufacturing the wrong kind of citizen. During the
[loyalty oath
controversies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_loyalty_oath_controversy)
of the McCarthy era, regents demanded professors swear anti-communist oaths or
lose their jobs. A decade later the fear flipped content but kept its shape,
as 1960s campus unrest convinced an older generation that universities were
radicalizing students against the country. In the1960s Vice-President Spiro
Agnew and eventually California Governor Ronald Reagan declared the same.

In 2025, President Trump [accused
faculty](https://thehill.com/opinion/education/5601601-college-indoctrination-
myth-exposed/) of turning students into “communists, terrorists and
sympathizers of many, many dimensions.” The same loyalty oath logic in new
packaging. What changes is which politics the university stands accused of
manufacturing. What does not change is the fear that it is secretly converting
the young into someone their parents would not recognize.

What should we make of complaints this durable? One possibility is that they
are simply true, and have been true since the Grant administration, without
higher education ever actually collapsing. That seems unlikely, given how much
of modern science, medicine, law, and technology has come out of these same
institutions in the meantime. The more interesting possibility is that these
complaints are not really about facts at all. They are about anxiety:
generational anxiety about whether the young are working hard enough, economic
anxiety about whether a credential still buys what it used to, and political
anxiety about who gets to shape the next generation's convictions.

None of this means today's version is wrong. Grades really have risen sharply,
and the labor market really has grown skeptical of degrees that do not map
onto a specific job. But history should make us humble about the diagnosis. If
Erasmus was mocking impractical scholars in 1509, and Harvard's faculty was
writing panicked memos about grade inflation while the ink was still drying on
the telephone patent, then the problem, whatever it is, is not a symptom of
any particular decade's decline. It is a permanent feature of how institutions
age, and how societies argue with themselves about what education is actually
for.

Additionally, largely ignored in all this is how corporate America has largely
captured higher education, remaking it in its own image in terms of structure
and organization. If higher education is failing it is because it is simply
serving the narrow interests of capitalism.

Finally, grade inflation is a problem, but the declining quality of higher
education speaks more to efforts by the Trump administration to censor
academic freedom, restrict admission by foreign students, or by states such as
Florida and Texas dictating curriculum. And let us not forget how elite
schools such as Harvard continue to give away admissions to legacy students
such that one can hardly say that they are accepting the best and the
brightest or awarding grades on the basis of merit.
